t: Number of Pairs of Interchangeable Rectangles: Grouping by Exact Ratio
o: Two rectangles are interchangeable when their width-to-height ratios match exactly, and we must count such pairs among up to 100000 rectangles. In [[4,8],[3,6],[10,20],[15,30]] every entry reduces to the ratio 1:2, and four rectangles sharing one ratio contribute C(4,2) = 6 pairs; in [[4,5],[7,8]] the ratios differ, so the answer is 0. Comparing all pairs costs about ten billion operations at the constraint ceiling, so the plan is to group by an exact, collision-free representation of each ratio: the fraction reduced by gcd, never a floating-point quotient that could round two distinct ratios together.
k: w1/h1 = w2/h2 holds exactly when the fractions reduced by gcd(w,h) are identical numerator-denominator pairs.
Never compare floating-point ratios for equality; integer reduction is exact and cheap.
While sweeping, the number of earlier rectangles with the current key is precisely the number of new pairs formed, enabling a one-pass accumulation.
The answer can reach roughly five billion pairs, so accumulate in 64-bit integers (a regular JavaScript number still suffices below 2^53).

a.i: Ratio equality w1/h1 = w2/h2 is equivalent to the integer cross product w1*h2 = w2*h1, which avoids any precision issue while staying dead simple. Check all C(n,2) pairs and count matches. Correct and a fine warm-up, but quadratic work cannot survive n = 10^5.
s: Loop i over all rectangles and j over indices after i.
Compare width_i * height_j against width_j * height_i using 64-bit products.
Increment the answer on equality and return it.
a.t: O(n^2) pair comparisons, around ten billion operations at n = 10^5, far too slow for the constraints.

a.n: Approach 2: Hash Map over Reduced Ratios
a.i: Group rectangles by their ratio in canonical form: divide both dimensions by gcd(w, h) and use the reduced pair as a hash key. Sweeping once, the count of earlier rectangles carrying the same key equals the number of new pairs the current rectangle forms, so adding that before inserting keeps a running total. This is linear up to gcd cost and needs only 64-bit accumulation.
s: For each rectangle compute g = gcd(w, h) and reduce to (w/g, h/g).
Encode the pair as a single map key, e.g., rw * 100001 + rh, or a string key.
Add the number of previously seen rectangles with this key to the answer.
Then increment the stored count for the key.
a.t: O(n log W) since each rectangle costs one gcd reduction plus O(1) hash operations.
a.sp: O(n) for at most one map entry per distinct ratio.

w: Reach for the reduced-fraction hash map immediately; the brute force is only a warm-up to state the problem. Pitfalls: trusting floating-point division for equality, accumulating the answer in 32-bit integers when it can exceed 2^31, and forgetting that identical rectangles also pair with each other. Natural follow-ups: count pairs whose ratios fall within some epsilon (sort by value and sweep), or enumerate the actual pairs for small inputs.
